When I joined Motorsport Network as CRO in 2019, there was no CRM. Not a broken one. Not an underused one. None. A ~$100M ARR business running on spreadsheets, tribal knowledge, and weekly calls where the forecast was whatever the senior rep said it was with enough conviction.
I built one and stood it up across 15 offices, unified the adtech stack, implemented KPIs that didn’t exist before. Within twelve months, forecast accuracy doubled. Revenue grew 25%. Not because we hired better salespeople. Not because the market got easier. Because for the first time, the business could actually see what was happening in its pipeline before the quarter closed.
That experience is what CSA is built on. The insight wasn’t that Motorsport needed a CRM. It was that a $100M business had been running blind — and the moment it could read its own signals, commercial performance changed materially and fast.
A reporting system tells you what happened. It takes outputs — ARR, NRR, churn rate, pipeline coverage — and displays them. It’s backward-looking by design. It answers the board’s questions after the quarter closes.
A revenue operating system tells you what’s about to happen. It reads signals — behavioral, conversational, financial, product-usage — before they become outcomes. It creates conditions to intervene when intervention is still possible. And critically: it doesn’t require new tools. It requires a different architecture layered over the tools you already have.
Here’s what the Motorsport numbers looked like before and after the signal infrastructure was in place.
I saw the same dynamic at a different scale at a Bain Capital-backed ad intelligence business where I served as CCO. The total commercial result was 52% YoY revenue growth. But the part I can specifically attribute to rebuilding segmentation and pipeline architecture — getting the business aimed at the right accounts with the right signal about who was actually converting — was roughly 10 points of that growth. In a $30M+ EBITDA business, 10 points is not a rounding error.
And earlier this year, an AI-native fintech with strong product-market fit but a pipeline that wasn’t moving. The issue: effort distributed evenly across a prospect universe regardless of conversion probability. No ICP framework. No tiering. No signal about where to aim.
CSA is the operating model that connects raw commercial signals to board-level outcomes. It runs across four layers: 1) the systems that capture signals; 2) the humans who own them; 3) the processes that act on them; and 4) the reporting that makes them visible to leadership and investors.
It is not a tool recommendation. It is not a RevOps engagement. It is not a twelve-week project after which you hand over a deck and leave. It is the connective tissue between your commercial stack and your commercial results — and once it’s running, it changes how the company operates permanently, not just how it reports this quarter.
Every piece of commercial signal — a deal going quiet, a champion changing jobs, a support ticket spike, a seat utilization drop — has to survive five stages before it can influence a decision:
Over the next eleven weeks I’m publishing the complete CSA framework — built and deployed across Motorsport Network (GMF Capital), Vivvix (Bain Capital), Recurrent Ventures (Blackstone), and BrightRoll (acquired by Yahoo).
Each week covers one layer or one application: raw signals and how to read them, the systems layer and where AI actually belongs in it, the human layer and why signal breaks down in your org chart, process design, the board questions CSA is built to answer, and implementation sequencing for PE-backed companies without a data team. Specific throughout — named signal types, named gap patterns, real numbers where I can use them.
If the answer is “we saw it in the data after it happened,” you have a reporting system, not an operating system. That’s what this series is for.
